The RDC statistic is constructed in three steps:

1. Apply a copula transformation to each of the two random samples. [8]

The authors’ point is that HGR is not a practical quantity to compute exactly: it takes a supremum over an infinite-dimensional class of functions, making it computationally intractable and merely an abstract dependence concept [1]. The supplied passage also indicates that an exact finite-dataset approximation is “not desirable,” although the excerpt cuts off before stating the authors’ specific finite-sample reason [8].

Instead, RDC uses a scalable, finite-dimensional approximation in the spirit of HGR [2][3]. It applies random nonlinear projections to empirical copula transformations and measures dependence as the largest canonical correlation between those projections [4][5]. This makes it lightweight and scalable, with approximately \(O(n\log n)\) dependence on sample size [7].

They argue that the approximations used by these methods are exact only if the selected features satisfy two conditional-independence assumptions: their joint conditional entropy can be decomposed into pairwise terms when conditioning on a candidate feature, and likewise when conditioning on that feature **and** the response \(y\) [4].  

Those assumptions are generally incompatible because conditioning on \(y\) can create dependencies among the features. Thus, if the second conditional-independence assumption holds, the first will generally fail, except under a very specific—and unrealistic—data-generating structure [7][8]. Moreover, in that exceptional structure the candidate feature \(x_i\) would be more informative about \(y\) than the already selected feature set, meaning it should have been selected earlier and contradicting the selection process [7].
question_answers.fetch-012:
In the Pairwise Q-distribution, the conditional for the new feature is formed as the geometric mean of its pairwise class-conditional distributions with the previously selected features:

\[
q(x_{f_t}\mid x_{f_{<t}},y)
=
\left(\prod_{i=1}^{t-1} p(x_{f_t}\mid x_{f_i},y)\right)^{1/(t-1)}.
\]

This construction can be updated recursively: when a new feature is added, the previous \(q\)-conditional is combined with the new pairwise conditional and renormalized by the new number of features [5]. The authors justify this choice as a tractable alternative that is more general than the Naive Bayes Q-distribution, while still fitting the autoregressive, one-feature-at-a-time forward-selection procedure [6][7].

The reduction assumes that, for a candidate feature \(X_i\), the remaining selected features \(X_{S_i}=S\setminus\{X_i\}\) are both conditionally independent given \(X_i\) and class-conditionally independent given \((X_i,Y)\):

\[
p(X_{S_i}\mid X_i)=\prod_{j\in S_i}p(X_j\mid X_i),\qquad
p(X_{S_i}\mid X_i,Y)=\prod_{j\in S_i}p(X_j\mid X_i,Y).
\]

[8]

Under this assumption, the subset–class mutual information reduces to

\[
I(X_S;Y)
=
I(X_i;Y)
+
\sum_{X_j\in S_i} I(X_j;Y\mid X_i),
\]

so it can be estimated using pairwise conditional mutual-information terms involving \(X_i\), \(X_j\), and \(Y\). [8][3]

VMR_mRMR preserves several pieces of state across iterations:

- The **relevance score of every feature**, since relevance depends only on the decision variable and not on the selected-feature subset, so it can be cached and reused. [5]
- The **selected-feature state** (`sF`), including the most recently selected feature, which is used for subsequent redundancy calculations. [6]
- The **cached and accumulated redundancy/mRMR contributions** associated with each candidate feature. [1]

Thus, each iteration does not recompute all relevance and pairwise redundancy terms. It computes the conditional-entropy/MI contribution for the currently available candidate features: with the decision variable in the first iteration, and thereafter only with the most recently selected feature. [8] Those newly computed values are accumulated into the candidates’ scores, after which the best candidate according to mRMR is selected and added to the selected set. [1]

It avoids the contingency tables or histograms used by earlier vertical approaches because those structures are computationally intensive and consume more space—up to \(|dom(F_i)| \times |dom(F)|\) entries [8]. Restricting computation to `possiblePairs` avoids redundant calculations and reduces the required storage [8].

question_answers.operator-001: Filter methods select variables independently of the forecasting/classification algorithm, typically by ranking their predictive strength and applying a threshold before prediction; the resulting subset can be used with different algorithms and is relatively simple to understand [3][4][6][7][8]. Wrapper methods, by contrast, use a particular mining or forecasting algorithm as a black-box evaluator and search for the subset that maximizes that algorithm’s performance, accounting for feature dependencies [1][6][8]. Thus, wrappers may achieve better, algorithm-specific performance, but they are computationally slower and their selected subset may not transfer well to other algorithms [1][2].

After that, variables are added incrementally: previously selected variables remain in the set, and at each step the unselected feature maximizing

\[
I(X_i;Y)-\frac{1}{|S|}\sum_{X_j\in S} I(X_j;X_i)
\]

is added—that is, the feature with the greatest relevance to the target minus its average redundancy with the already selected variables [3].

Ding and Peng converted each gene’s continuous expression values into categorical states using that gene’s sample mean \(\mu\) and standard deviation \(\sigma\). Values greater than \(\mu+\sigma/2\) were assigned state **1**; values between \(\mu-\sigma/2\) and \(\mu+\sigma/2\) were assigned state **0**; and values below \(\mu-\sigma/2\) were assigned state **−1**. [6][8] They also tested alternative discretization settings producing two- or three-state variables before applying MRMR. [5]

Biologically, the three states represent **over-expression** (1), **baseline expression** (0), and **under-expression** (−1) relative to the gene’s own sample distribution. [8] This made the measurements categorical, allowing mutual information to quantify gene similarity and redundancy. [4]

Instead, they use a simple greedy heuristic: select the first feature with the highest mutual information/relevance to the target, then add features incrementally from the remaining set while retaining the features already selected [8].

question_answers.operator-013:
The Randomized Dependence Coefficient (RDC) measures dependence as the maximum correlation between linear combinations of randomized nonlinear copula projections of the two variables:

\[
\operatorname{rdc}(X,Y;k,s)
=
\sup_{\alpha,\beta}
\rho\!\left(
\alpha^T\Phi_{k,s}(X),
\beta^T\Phi_{k,s}(Y)
\right).
\]

Here, \(k\) and \(s\) control the randomized projections. [3][4] It is therefore a finite-dimensional, nonlinear dependence measure inspired by the HGR maximum correlation coefficient. [1][2][7]

For random variables with dimensions \(p\) and \(q\), its computational cost is \(O((p+q)^2 n)\), where \(n\) is the sample size. Thus, for fixed \(p\) and \(q\), the cost grows linearly with \(n\). [3][4]
question_answers.operator-014: RDC uses the empirical copula transformation to remove the effects of the variables’ marginal distributions, so the dependence measure is invariant to monotonically increasing transformations such as shifts or rescalings [8]. The transformation maps each variable through its empirical CDF, producing uniformized values that preserve the variables’ dependence structure while discarding marginal-scale information [1][8]. RDC can then apply random nonlinear projections and compute the largest canonical correlation on this standardized dependence representation [6]. Operating directly on raw samples would make the result sensitive to arbitrary marginal scales and transformations [7][8].

question_answers.operator-019:
In mRMR, for a candidate feature \(X_i\), let \(Y\) be the target/class variable and \(S\) the set of already selected features:

- **MID (Mutual Information Difference):**
  \[
  f_{\mathrm{MID}}(X_i)
  = I(Y;X_i)-\frac{1}{|S|}\sum_{X_s\in S} I(X_s;X_i)
  \]
  It maximizes relevance to \(Y\) while subtracting the feature’s average redundancy with the selected features. [7]

- **MIQ (Mutual Information Quotient):**
  \[
  f_{\mathrm{MIQ}}(X_i)
  =\frac{I(Y;X_i)}
  {\frac{1}{|S|}\sum_{X_s\in S} I(X_s;X_i)}
  \]
  It balances relevance and redundancy through a ratio rather than a difference. [7]

Thus, **MID uses subtraction**, whereas **MIQ uses division**; both seek high relevance and low redundancy. [7][8]
question_answers.operator-020:
The authors chose the arithmetic mean because it preserved evidence from all time points while still producing a meaningful overall relevance score. Although the median is more robust to outliers, it can miss genes whose group differences occur during only a short portion of the observed period, such as a few time points with large F-statistics followed by several small ones [6][4]. In contrast, the arithmetic mean may be lowered by small F-statistics but can still remain significant in this situation [8].

They also tested multilayer aggregation, which combines the arithmetic mean, geometric mean, and median, but found that it did not significantly improve the results and reduced the robustness of the feature-selection methods [5][7]. Therefore, they selected the arithmetic mean as the most suitable and robust operator for summarizing F-statistics across all time steps [7].
question_answers.operator-021: Z-score normalization is applied because DTW can miss similarity between time series that have similar fluctuations but different offsets or amplitudes—for example, signals varying between 5–10 versus 30–40 [1]. Normalization removes these offset and amplitude differences, making the series fluctuate around zero and differ primarily in shape [6]. This allows the DTW distance matrix to measure the shape-based similarity relevant for assessing redundancy between genes [6][7].

fast-mRMR applies several optimizations to original mRMR:

- **A greedy feature-selection approach** limits the number of feature-to-feature comparisons by considering how many features must ultimately be selected [4]. This transforms mRMR’s quadratic process into a more efficient greedy process [8].
- **Caching relevant information:** quantities such as mutual-information values are calculated once and reused in later iterations, avoiding repeated calculations [5].
- **An optimized data-access pattern** improves the performance of mutual-information computations and overall execution [7][8].

The data-access optimization changes the layout from the usual **row-wise storage**—where samples are the primary contiguous units—to a **feature-wise layout**, so values belonging to the same feature are stored/accessed together. This reduces costly random access, which is especially important on GPUs [5].

MRmMC treats redundancy as the **multicollinearity introduced when a candidate feature is added to the already selected subset**.[2] Its criterion combines relevance with this redundancy measure, aiming to balance the two without a user-specified control parameter.[2] The measure is intended to capture linear relationships and, in some cases, nonlinear relationships between quantitative features.[5]

However, the supplied passages do **not** state the mathematical formula or algorithm used to compute MRmMC’s multicollinearity value. They only say that it is evaluated when the candidate is added to the selected subset.[2] The explicit computation shown elsewhere—averaging pairwise mutual information over the selected features—is the mRMR computation, not explicitly MRmMC:  
\[
\mathrm{Red}(X_j,S)=\frac{1}{|S|}\sum_{X_s\in S} I(X_j;X_s),
\]
followed by relevance minus redundancy.[8]

The authors acknowledge two main limitations:

- **Candidate-subset formation:** ImRMR first divides features into candidate subsets using an **equal grouping method (EGM)**, so the subsets depend on this initial grouping rather than being formed by exhaustively evaluating every possible feature combination [8]. This matters because feature-selection methods can miss the joint contribution of multiple features when they focus on individual features or limited combinations [3][5].

- **Relevance and redundancy measurement:** ImRMR calculates subset contribution using **Pearson correlation and mutual information** [8]. The authors note that using different measures for relevance and redundancy can put them on different scales, which affects the trade-off between the two criteria [4]. They also acknowledge that some redundancy measures may be reliable for quantitative variables but ineffective for measuring redundancy between quantitative and nominal variables [1].
question_answers.operator-042:
The **Randomized Dependence Coefficient (RDC)** is a lightweight, nonlinear measure of dependence between random variables of arbitrary dimension, designed as a finite-dimensional estimator inspired by the HGR maximum correlation coefficient [5][7].

Given samples \(X\) and \(Y\), RDC computes

\[
\operatorname{RDC}(X,Y;k,s)
=
\sup_{\alpha,\beta}
\rho\!\left(
\alpha^\top \Phi(P(X);k,s),
\beta^\top \Phi(P(Y);k,s)
\right),
\]

where \(P(\cdot)\) denotes the copula/rank transformation and \(\Phi\) denotes randomized nonlinear features [2][3]. Thus, the quantity it actually computes is the **maximum Pearson correlation—equivalently, the first canonical correlation—between linear projections of randomized nonlinear transformations of the two variables** [2][7]. It is therefore an estimator of HGR-style maximal correlation, not mutual information or a generic probability of dependence [1][2].

In all three, the first feature is selected by **relevance alone**, not by the combined relevance–redundancy score:

- **Microarray MRMR paper:** It explicitly says, “The best feature according to relevance is selected” and used as the reference for the redundancy phase; the mRMR criterion is applied to the remaining features [5].
- **Fast-mRMR:** It first computes and caches relevance values, then selects “the best feature according to relevance” before entering the iterative redundancy-processing steps [6].
- **TMRMR:** Its criterion subtracts redundancy with respect to the already selected set \(S\). At the initial step, there are no selected features, so the redundancy term is absent and the choice reduces to maximizing relevance [8].

Thus, the combined criterion governs selections from the **second feature onward**.
